newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Latin Americans lobby for U.N. human rights post.
newsitem.headline: Latin Americans lobby for U.N. human rights post.

text.p: Latin American nations are pressing U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan to choose a new human rights commissioner from their continent rather than turn to a European, such as Irish President Mary Robinson, diplomats say.

The post became open after Jose Ayala Lasso of Ecuador resigned earlier this month as the first U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights to become his country's foreign minister. He was appointed in 1994 for a four-year term and at least three women are ready to replace him.

Latin American delegates argue that at minimum a candidate from their region should be appointed to complete Ayala Lasso's term for another year and several developing nations agree, contending that the West has more than its share of senior U.N. posts.

High on the list is Sonia Picado, Costa Rica's ambassador to Washington. She is an author, the first woman judge in her country and the first woman in Latin America to be elected dean of a law school, envoys said.

Another frequently mentioned name is Paulo Sergio Pinheiro, a Brazilian lawyer who serves as U.N. special rapporteur (investigator) on Burundi, and the drafter of landmark 1996 human rights legislation in his country.

Outside of Latin America, the Phillipines is expected to nominate Purificacion Quinsumbing, currently Ayala Lasso's representative in New York, a former assistant foreign minister and a longtime rights advocate.
And Elisabeth Rehn, the special U.N. rapporteur for human rights in the former Yugoslavia, and Finland's former defence minister is also said to be seeking the post.

Robinson, who announced earlier this month that she would not seek a second seven-year term as president of Ireland, has been nominated by her government for the job. She ends her presidency at the end of the year and is credited with changing a largely ceremonial post into a platform for domestic and foreign affairs, particularly on human rights.
Speculation was rife that Robinson made her wishes public after encouragement by Annan and that he would keep the post open until she finished her term in December.

But U.N. officials denied any promises were made, saying he had not made a decision yet and would probably not do so for several weeks. The post has to be approved by the U.N. General Assembly, where developing nations hold a majority.

The high commissioner's job had been proposed since 1947 but was not approved until late in 1993 due to compromises forged by Ayalo Lasso, then Ecuador's ambassdor and head of General Assembly committee. He was then named to the job.

The West wanted an outspoken rights commissioner with investigatory powers while some Third World countries wanted probes restricted. Consequently, the resolution creating the job is purposely vague in spelling out the post's duties.
Ayala Lasso, whose Geneva-based office is short of funds and understaffed, has been criticised for his low-profile.

"He gave up the key force he has to defend human rights -- which is the willingness to publicly condemn abusive governments," said Kenneth Roth, executive director of the New York-based Human Rights Watch. "He insisted on using quiet diplomacy when he had no clout to privately deliver."
In Rwanda, diplomats say his successful deployment of more than 130 observers following 1994's Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis prevented retaliatory massacres.
He is also credited with holding his ground on Cuba, saying that the 30-year trade embargo had not worked.
